paragraphs: Recording several brain regions at once creates an opportunity to study how they communicate. The difficulty is separating communication between recorded regions from activity generated within each region and influences arriving from regions that were not recorded. A model that mixes these sources can give a misleading account of interactions.

MR-LFADS addresses this separation using a sequential variational autoencoder with a recurrent network for each region. Its design combines structured information bottlenecks, communication constrained by the recorded data, and unsupervised inference of unobserved inputs. Together, these features support distinct explanations for local dynamics, communication between regions, and outside influences.

Across dozens of simulations involving task-trained networks with multiple regions, MR-LFADS identified communication better than existing approaches. On large-scale electrophysiology data, it also predicted brain-wide responses to circuit perturbations absent from model fitting. These results provide both simulated and real-data support for the approach, suggesting that it could help investigate how information processing is coordinated across the brain.
icml-2025-accurate-identification-of-com.tldr: MR-LFADS separates several sources of neural activity to better identify communication between brain regions.

paragraphs: Markov chain Monte Carlo methods generate samples by repeatedly proposing moves through a target distribution. Many commonly used methods have a step size that controls those moves. Choosing it is difficult when different parts of the distribution have different scales: a setting that works well in one region may work poorly elsewhere.

AutoStep selects a step size at each iteration according to the target distribution's local geometry. It applies to methods built around deterministic involutive proposals, a class of transformations that reverse themselves when applied twice. The central contribution is to make local adaptation part of a sampling procedure with theoretical support.

Under mild conditions, the authors prove that AutoStep preserves the target distribution and is irreducible and aperiodic. They also bound expected energy jump distance and computational cost per iteration. Experiments on challenging distributions find competitive effective sample sizes per unit cost relative to leading methods. The findings support local step-size selection as a practical way to handle distributions for which one global setting may be inadequate.
icml-2025-autostep-locally-adaptive-invo.tldr: AutoStep adapts MCMC step sizes to local geometry while preserving key sampling properties under mild conditions.

paragraphs: Survival analysis models when an event will happen, using data that can include censored observations whose event times are not fully observed. This paper examines how variational inference behaves in latent-variable models for that setting. Its concern is that an unsuitable approximation can interfere with learning the time-to-event distribution itself.

The authors prove that the optimal variational distribution, which makes the likelihood bound exact, may depend on the censoring mechanism. This is a conditional finding: it identifies censoring as something the inference design may need to accommodate. Their proposed censor-dependent variational inference, or CDVI, explicitly tailors the approximation to survival analysis.

For scalable implementation, the paper introduces CD-CVAE, a variational autoencoder with a V-shaped dependency structure. It also extends existing theory and training techniques to this setting. Experiments support the analysis and show significant improvements in estimating individual survival distributions. The contribution therefore connects the design of approximate inference directly to the quality of the event-time distributions that survival models are meant to learn.
icml-2025-censor-dependent-variational-i.tldr: CDVI accounts for possible censoring dependence in variational inference to improve individual survival-distribution estimates.

paragraphs: Vision-language models often adapt language-model architectures by aligning visual features with language representations. The paper identifies two problems with this design. As context grows, attention increasingly neglects visual content in the middle. Conventional positional encodings also fail to retain important two-dimensional relationships when handling images at dynamic high resolutions.

CoMemo introduces two paths for processing images: a context image path and an image memory path. This arrangement alleviates the neglect of visual information. A complementary positional encoding, RoPE-DHR, aggregates positions using thumbnails to preserve spatial awareness while reducing the weakening of relationships across distant positions in long sequences.

Evaluations cover seven benchmarks spanning long-context comprehension, reasoning across multiple images, and visual question answering. CoMemo performs better than conventional vision-language architectures in these tests. The results support addressing both how visual information remains available and how its spatial layout is represented. These are related but distinct architectural issues that become especially relevant as image content and context length increase.
icml-2025-comemo-lvlms-need-image-contex.tldr: CoMemo combines image context, image memory, and spatial positional encoding to improve vision-language processing.

paragraphs: Helpfulness votes are useful for ranking online content, but their totals reflect more than content quality. Position affects whether people encounter an item, and existing votes can influence later voters. The paper studies how to account for these contextual effects when estimating which content users actually find valuable.

Counterfactual Voting Adjustment, or CVA, uses a causal framework to model the circumstances surrounding individual votes. Preliminary and semi-synthetic experiments test its treatment of position and herding biases against predefined content quality. In those settings, CVA models the biases effectively and accurately recovers the quality values used to construct the evaluation.

In a real experiment, rankings based on CVA's learned quality align more closely with user sentiment and GPT-4o quality assessments than aggregate-vote rankings or model-based rerankings without causal inference. This provides evidence for the adjustment through those particular evaluation signals. The learned embeddings also support comparisons of expert-user behavior across 120 major StackExchange communities, extending the analysis beyond individual content rankings.
icml-2025-counterfactual-voting-adjustme.tldr: CVA adjusts for position and herding effects in helpfulness votes to estimate content quality more fairly.

paragraphs: Giving a language model additional reasoning steps can improve difficult answers, but generating those steps as text can add latency and complicate optimization. This paper explores an alternative place for extra computation: the model's key-value cache, which stores internal representations used during subsequent token generation.

The method adds a coprocessor that produces latent embeddings to augment that cache. Training uses the decoder's language-modeling loss on ordinary pretraining data, while the decoder remains frozen. This makes the extra computation differentiable end to end and teaches the coprocessor to place useful information directly into the cache.

Because the decoder itself is unchanged, the coprocessor can run offline and asynchronously. The language model can also continue operating when the coprocessor is unavailable or extra computation is unnecessary. Experiments show lower perplexity across numerous tokens following augmentation and consistent improvements on several reasoning-intensive tasks without task-specific training. These findings indicate that additional internal computation can improve later decoding without expressing every intermediate step as generated text.
icml-2025-deliberation-in-latent-space-v.tldr: A trained coprocessor augments a frozen language model's cache with latent embeddings that improve subsequent predictions and reasoning.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks process information through discrete events and offer an energy-efficient alternative to conventional artificial neural networks. Converting an existing network into this form can lose accuracy or require more inference time. The paper targets three sources of conversion error: clipping, quantization, and uneven activation.

Its error-compensation framework assigns a mechanism to each problem. A learnable threshold clipping function adapts thresholds to reduce clipping error. Dual-threshold neurons dynamically reduce quantization error. An optimized initialization of membrane potentials addresses uneven activation by managing the internal state from which spiking neurons begin processing.

Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet report high accuracy with very low latency among conversion methods. In one concrete result, a converted ResNet-18 reaches 94.75% accuracy on CIFAR-10 using only two time steps. This demonstrates competitive accuracy with a short processing window in that setting. The findings support the approach as a route toward practical real-time processing on low-power hardware by reducing the errors that otherwise make rapid conversion-based inference difficult.
icml-2025-efficient-ann-snn-conversion-w.tldr: Targeted error compensation enables accurate ANN-to-SNN conversion with very few inference time steps.

paragraphs: Partial dependence describes how selected input features affect a trained model's predictions after averaging over the other features. It underlies several interpretation methods, including partial-dependence plots and SHAP. The paper highlights a tension: efficient SHAP estimation is available, but a single contribution can combine a feature's main effect with its interactions.

FastPD is a tree-based estimator for partial-dependence functions involving arbitrary feature subsets. This broader target allows the same estimation machinery to support individual feature effects and higher-order interactions. The authors prove consistency for the desired population quantity, contrasting it with path-dependent TreeSHAP, which is inconsistent when features are correlated.

For moderately deep trees, FastPD reduces the dependence on the number of observations from quadratic to linear relative to existing methods. That qualification matters because the computational claim is tied to tree depth. The method can produce SHAP values, partial-dependence plots, and interaction effects. Its contribution is thus both computational and interpretive: it makes a wider range of dependence-based explanations available through efficient, statistically consistent estimation.
icml-2025-fast-estimation-of-partial-dep.tldr: FastPD efficiently and consistently estimates partial dependence for tree models, supporting feature effects and higher-order interactions.

paragraphs: Generalized category discovery uses labeled examples from known classes to identify unlabeled examples that may belong to either known or new classes. Parametric approaches avoid costly clustering during inference, but unreliable self-supervision can weaken their ability to distinguish the known classes. Improving those classes must also avoid increasing bias against new ones.

The proposed Reciprocal Learning Framework adds an auxiliary branch dedicated to known-class classification. The main branch selects unlabeled samples believed to belong to known classes and passes them to this auxiliary branch. In return, the auxiliary branch supplies more reliable soft labels, creating a training exchange intended to improve the main branch's supervision.

Class-wise Distribution Regularization complements that exchange by reducing bias toward known classes and increasing prediction confidence on unlabeled data. The combined method, RLCD, improves performance across known and new classes with negligible additional computation. Experiments across seven category-discovery datasets support its superiority. The approach matters because it treats reliable known-class supervision and successful new-class discovery as linked training problems that require complementary mechanisms.
icml-2025-generalized-category-discovery.tldr: RLCD combines reciprocal supervision and class-wise regularization to improve discovery of both known and novel categories.

paragraphs: Recovering missing locations in human movement records supports applications such as transportation and urban planning. Sparse observations make the task difficult because the model must capture relationships across both space and time. Existing recurrent and attention-based methods face challenges with these dependencies, while diffusion models typically generate continuous representations rather than location sequences directly.

DiffMove bridges that representation mismatch by converting locations into embeddings. A conditional diffusion process denoises those embeddings, and an embedding decoder turns the resulting representations into recovered locations. The method also models movement transitions, periodic behavior, and temporal patterns, giving the recovery process structure specific to human mobility.

Experiments on two real-world mobility datasets report significant improvements over the strongest baselines, including an average 11% improvement in recall. This supports the use of generative modeling for trajectory recovery in the evaluated settings. The central idea is to perform diffusion in a representation where it can operate naturally, then translate its output back into locations while accounting for recurring patterns in how people move.
icml-2025-generative-human-trajectory-re.tldr: DiffMove recovers missing trajectory locations through conditional diffusion over embeddings that capture human mobility patterns.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning can train heterogeneous graph models without labels, but contrastive approaches often require carefully designed graph augmentations and positive-negative sample choices. Deciding how similar two samples should be is itself difficult. HGOT addresses these design burdens using optimal transport to relate different semantic views of the graph.

The method constructs branch views from different meta-paths and an aggregating central view that integrates their semantic information. An optimal transport plan then identifies relationships between the semantics of each branch and the central view. Aligning these transport relationships with the learned representations encourages the encoder to capture the graph's structure more faithfully.

HGOT avoids graph augmentation strategies and eases the sampling process associated with contrastive learning. Experiments on four real-world datasets report state-of-the-art performance across downstream tasks, with average node-classification accuracy improvements exceeding 6% relative to leading methods. These results support learning through alignment among graph views as a useful alternative to relying on manually designed augmentations and selected pairs of similar or dissimilar samples.
icml-2025-hgot-self-supervised-heterogen.tldr: HGOT uses optimal transport to align heterogeneous graph views and learn useful node representations without graph augmentation.

paragraphs: The paper studies selecting a useful subset while keeping its total cost within a budget. Its objective is monotone and submodular: adding items does not reduce value, and additional items have diminishing returns. This setting includes maximum coverage, influence maximization, and feature selection, where evolutionary methods already offer promising practical performance.

The authors first revisit POMC, an existing multi-objective evolutionary algorithm. A new analysis raises its approximation guarantee from one-half times one minus one over e to one-half. This is a stronger theoretical guarantee for the existing algorithm, helping explain its encouraging empirical performance without requiring a change to the method itself.

The paper then introduces EPOL, a new multi-objective evolutionary algorithm with a 0.6174 approximation guarantee, described as the best-known practical guarantee. It also reports superior empirical performance on maximum coverage and influence maximization. Together, the results strengthen both the theoretical case for evolutionary subset selection and its demonstrated effectiveness, narrowing the gap between favorable practical behavior and what analysis can guarantee under the stated objective and cost constraints.
icml-2025-improved-theoretically-grounde.tldr: A stronger analysis of POMC and the new EPOL algorithm improve guarantees for budget-constrained submodular subset selection.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a language model on high-quality reasoning data can be effective, but updating every parameter is expensive and can cause overfitting or forgetting when data is limited. Sparse fine-tuning reduces the number of updated weights. Its central challenge is identifying which weights are useful for improving reasoning.

The paper identifies principal weights as those with the largest magnitudes after a low-rank approximation. Its key observation is that magnitude-based selection becomes effective after this rank reduction, despite performing poorly as a direct selection rule. LIFT uses that information to update only the top 5% of principal weights throughout training.

In the reported experiments, LIFT consistently exceeds full fine-tuning on reasoning tasks while matching the memory efficiency of popular parameter-efficient methods. It performs strongly on domains such as arithmetic reasoning and retains up to 20% more source-domain knowledge than full fine-tuning and LoRA. These results suggest that the representation used to identify important weights can substantially affect sparse fine-tuning's balance of adaptation, memory use, and knowledge retention.
icml-2025-lift-the-veil-for-the-truth-pr.tldr: LIFT uses low-rank approximation to select the 5% of weights it updates, improving reasoning and knowledge retention in reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Large language model pretraining consumes substantial computational resources. This paper asks whether intermediate checkpoints can provide additional value beyond their role as snapshots along the training process. The proposed strategy combines checkpoints that share a training trajectory, seeking to make better use of computation already invested in producing them.

The central optimization problem is choosing the merging weight. The authors use Bayesian optimization to explore that search space and identify a favorable combination. A held-out dataset is required for the method. This connects checkpoint merging to an explicit search procedure rather than treating the choice of combination weight as incidental.

Across various experiments, the strategy shows potential to improve pretraining at comparatively small additional cost. The authors also report robust generalization across diverse domains despite using a particular held-out dataset. That finding matters because pretraining improvements need to carry beyond the data used to select a merge. The contribution is therefore a way to extract further usefulness from related intermediate models, with experimental evidence supporting both gains and cross-domain generalization.
icml-2025-maximizing-intermediate-checkp.tldr: Bayesian optimization selects weights for merging related pretraining checkpoints, yielding reported gains with robust cross-domain generalization.

paragraphs: Relationships involving several variables can contain structure that pairwise comparisons do not capture. Kernel-based hypothesis tests offer a flexible way to investigate these higher-order relationships without choosing a fixed parametric model. Their computational bottleneck is often the repeated permutations used to approximate how a statistic behaves when the tested relationship is absent.

The paper introduces tests for joint independence and partial factorizations among multiple variables that avoid those permutations. It combines V-statistics with a new cross-centring technique. Under the null hypothesis, the resulting statistics have a standard normal limiting distribution, providing an asymptotic reference for testing without constructing a permutation-based approximation.

Implementations are evaluated on synthetic datasets to demonstrate effectiveness and scalability. The authors also present applications motivated by causal discovery and feature selection, where relationships among groups of variables can matter. The contribution is a computationally more scalable testing framework whose justification rests on a limiting distribution under the null. It makes higher-order statistical structure more accessible without the repeated reshuffling used by conventional permutation procedures.
icml-2025-permutation-free-high-order-in.tldr: New kernel tests detect higher-order dependence using an asymptotic normal reference instead of costly permutation approximations.

paragraphs: In a principal-agent bandit game, a principal learns about an unknown environment by rewarding an agent for taking actions. The agent has its own interests. This paper considers agents that also learn their reward estimates over time and may explore, making their responses harder to anticipate than those of fully informed greedy agents.

The authors develop an elimination framework with search procedures that account for uncertainty arising from the agent's learning. For a non-exploring learning agent, they obtain regret bounds scaling as the square root of the horizon in the independent, identically distributed reward setting and as the horizon to the two-thirds power in the linear setting, up to logarithmic factors.

A more robust version accommodates exploratory agents and obtains a two-thirds-power bound in the independent-reward setting. In a special case matching an earlier agent model, it improves the bound from an eleven-twelfths power to a square-root rate. These results distinguish the guarantees available under different reward and agent behaviors, showing how incentive design can accommodate an agent whose knowledge and actions evolve.
icml-2025-principal-agent-bandit-games-w.tldr: New incentive algorithms provide regret guarantees when self-interested agents learn their rewards and may explore.

paragraphs: Language-model theorem provers can use conventional automation to complete proofs, but earlier systems often apply it only when the model requests it or at one fixed level of detail. ProofAug examines the structure of proposed proofs so that automation can operate at several granularities, making more extensive use of existing proving tools.

The procedure is designed as a module that integrates with any tree-search algorithm. The authors use it to construct an efficient recursive proving module and also combine it with mixed prompting. This separates the model's generation of proof proposals from a structured process for finding opportunities to complete them automatically.

On miniF2F with Isabelle and deepseek-math-7b-base, the combined approach achieves cumulative pass rates of 66.0% after dataset curation and 61.9% on the original dataset using 2,100 model queries per problem. The stated prior Isabelle result is 56.1% with 16,384 queries. A Lean 4 implementation raises another model's pass@1 from 44.3% to 50.4%. These evaluations support both improved proving success and more effective use of model queries in the reported settings.
icml-2025-proofaug-efficient-neural-theo.tldr: ProofAug analyzes generated proof structure to apply automation at multiple granularities and improve theorem-proving performance.

paragraphs: Semi-structured pruning removes selected language-model weights in a patterned way to support faster serving. Choosing which weights to remove is crucial. The paper argues that existing methods make suboptimal choices because they rely on local, layer-by-layer heuristics and do not take sufficient advantage of feedback from the overall model.

ProxSparse treats mask selection as a learning problem using regularized optimization. It turns a rigid, non-differentiable choice into a smoother procedure that can explore candidate masks gradually. This creates flexibility during selection while targeting the semi-structured sparsity needed for acceleration. Once the mask is determined, the method does not perform additional weight updates.

Evaluations on seven widely used models show consistent, significant improvements over earlier semi-structured mask-selection methods. These findings support optimizing the pruning pattern with learned feedback rather than relying only on local selection rules. The contribution concerns the quality of the selected mask: it provides a way to improve pruning outcomes without adding a subsequent phase of weight updates after the pattern has been fixed.
icml-2025-proxsparse-regularized-learnin.tldr: ProxSparse learns semi-structured pruning masks through regularized optimization, improving selection without subsequent weight updates.

paragraphs: Binary preference labels record which response is better but can discard ties and distinctions such as a slight preference. This paper develops reward modeling with ordinal feedback, allowing judgments at arbitrary levels of granularity. The aim is to retain information that a simple winner-loser decision would otherwise remove.

The theoretical framework rests on a marginal unbiasedness condition that generalizes an assumption used for binary feedback. The authors validate this condition through the sociological idea of crowd wisdom. Under that condition, they construct a probability model and prove that finer feedback reduces Rademacher complexity, a measure relevant to controlling a model's ability to fit varying labels.

Numerical experiments find better reward-model learning with finer feedback both within and outside the training distribution. They also find benefits from including a certain proportion of tied samples. These results support collecting richer judgments rather than automatically excluding ambiguous comparisons. The framework additionally informs annotator guidelines and offers a possible connection to the bias-variance trade-off in knowledge distillation, while its theoretical benefits remain tied to the stated condition.
icml-2025-reward-modeling-with-ordinal-f.tldr: Ordinal feedback preserves preference strength and ties, improving reward learning with theoretical benefits under a marginal unbiasedness condition.

paragraphs: Finding a sparse generalized linear model and proving that it is optimal are different computational tasks. This paper studies certification when a cardinality constraint limits the number of nonzero coefficients. Branch-and-bound can establish optimality, but it relies on dual bounds whose computation can become a major obstacle at large scale.

The authors design a first-order proximal gradient algorithm for the perspective relaxation used inside branch-and-bound. They express the relaxation as a composite optimization problem and show that the nonsmooth component's proximal operator can be computed exactly in log-linear time. This avoids solving an expensive second-order cone program for that step.

A simple restart strategy improves convergence while retaining inexpensive iterations. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report substantially faster dual-bound computation and effective optimality certification for large problems. The practical significance is in strengthening the machinery used to rule out competing solutions: cheaper bounds help branch-and-bound certify a sparse model's optimality, rather than merely return a model that appears to fit well.
icml-2025-scalable-first-order-method-fo.tldr: An efficient proximal-gradient solver accelerates the dual bounds needed to certify optimal sparse generalized linear models.

paragraphs: Open-set grounded segmentation identifies image regions described by varied text expressions. Existing approaches often need substantial training and can produce inconsistent fragments when different expressions refer to a unified object. Segment Anyword addresses this using a training-free approach built around a frozen diffusion model.

The method extracts token-level cross-attention maps to form preliminary mask prompts, then refines them into object masks. Complex image-text relationships can make these prompts fragmented or noisy. A linguistic regularization step uses sentence dependencies and syntactic structure to bind and cluster visual prompts, making them more coherent and tolerant of noise.

The paper reports state-of-the-art results across different open-set segmentation tasks: 52.5 mIoU on Pascal Context 59, 67.73 cIoU on gRefCOCO, and 67.4 mIoU on GranDf. These findings support using language structure to improve the spatial signals already present in a frozen model. The approach matters because it combines existing visual-language attention with syntactic guidance to produce more consistent masks without requiring the extensive training associated with other approaches.
icml-2025-segment-anyword-mask-prompt-in.tldr: Segment Anyword uses frozen diffusion attention and linguistic structure to produce accurate text-grounded masks without training.

paragraphs: Object detection and instance segmentation need representations that capture both what an object is and where it is located. This paper develops self-supervised learning for a Vision Transformer with those joint requirements in mind. Its focus is on integrating positional information into feature learning rather than treating location as an incidental addition.

The method introduces positional encoding tied to the cropping process used in contrastive learning, with positions represented through a vector field. It also masks and predicts both content embeddings and positional embeddings of image patches in parallel. These two components encourage the model to learn intertwined representations of visual content and spatial position.

The authors pretrain on ImageNet-1K and then fine-tune for downstream tasks. On COCO object detection, their approach surpasses leading self-supervised methods while using fewer pretraining epochs. This supports the idea that richer positional learning can improve representations for dense prediction. The result connects the pretraining objective to the downstream need to recognize objects and localize them, rather than learning class-related content alone.
icml-2025-self-supervised-learning-of-in.tldr: Joint self-supervised learning of content and position improves object detection while requiring fewer pretraining epochs in the reported comparison.

paragraphs: Time series can retain fat-tailed distributions and changing statistical patterns even after stationarization. These properties can destabilize learned features, increase model variance, and make training harder. Morphing-Flow addresses the distribution presented to the forecasting network, aiming to normalize it while retaining the extreme values that carry useful information.

The framework combines Flow, a spline-based transformation layer, with Morph, a method trained at test time. Together they adapt nonstationary, fat-tailed inputs toward a structured, normal-like distribution within the network's effective activation range. The design explicitly seeks to preserve critical extreme features while adapting to distributional drift.

Experiments span eight datasets. With a linear backbone, the method matches leading models on datasets including Electricity and ETTh2. With a patch-based Mamba architecture, it improves on its closest competitor by 6.3% on average and reduces forecasting errors by 21.7% on Exchange. It also improves existing models as a plug-and-play module without architectural changes. These results support adaptive input normalization as a useful contributor to forecasting performance across the evaluated settings.
icml-2025-slimming-the-fat-tail-morphing.tldr: Morphing-Flow adaptively normalizes shifting, fat-tailed time series while preserving important extremes and improving forecasting.

paragraphs: Sundial is a family of foundation models for forecasting continuous-valued time series. Its central aim is to model the distribution of the next patch of observations, allowing multiple plausible futures. This provides a flexible representation of forecasting uncertainty while avoiding the need to convert numerical observations into discrete tokens.

The authors introduce TimeFlow Loss, based on flow matching, to pretrain adapted Transformers directly on time series. The models condition on histories of arbitrary length and are pretrained without specifying a prior distribution. Training uses TimeBench, a collection of one trillion time points drawn mostly from real-world datasets alongside synthetic data.

TimeFlow Loss mitigates mode collapse, supporting the generation of varied probable forecasts. The paper reports state-of-the-art results on both point and probabilistic forecasting benchmarks, strong scalability, and zero-shot predictions within a few milliseconds. These findings support the combination of large-scale pretraining and generative forecasting. The authors suggest that producing multiple plausible futures could improve reliability in real-world decisions, presenting that downstream benefit as a prospect rather than an established universal outcome.
icml-2025-sundial-a-family-of-highly-cap.tldr: Sundial uses flow-matching pretraining on continuous time series to generate multiple plausible forecasts with strong benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Off-policy reinforcement learning agents reuse stored experience through replay buffers. This improves sample efficiency when the data is informative and relevant to learning. Unproductive experience can instead complicate optimization and consume environment interactions, especially when an agent continues collecting redundant transitions during an episode that is no longer useful.

The paper frames the tendency to continue until an episode naturally ends as a form of sunk cost fallacy. Its learn-to-stop mechanism, LEAST, uses statistics derived from Q-values and gradients to guide early termination. These signals help the agent recognize when an episode is unproductive and stop collecting experience from it.

Evaluations across several reinforcement learning algorithms on MuJoCo and the DeepMind Control Suite show improved learning efficiency. The result supports making episode continuation part of the learning process rather than always waiting for natural termination. The proposed benefit depends on avoiding uninformative transitions: replay remains useful when stored experience supports the objective, while selective early stopping reduces the collection of data that can hinder progress.
icml-2025-the-courage-to-stop-overcoming.tldr: LEAST uses Q-value and gradient statistics to stop unproductive episodes early and improve reinforcement-learning efficiency.
